#project: # THE OPT-OUT for lib/verb-set.sh and bin/cut-verb-build.sh. Read by both and
# by nothing else. Every row is a WRITTEN JUDGEMENT that an executable on a
# `bashified` branch was never meant to be a verb, despite qualifying.
# THE RULE IT EXEMPTS FROM, SINCE #891
#   a project declares a verb  <=>  its `bashified` branch carries an
#   executable `bin/<name>`. A `man/<name>.1` beside it is carried when
#   present and is never a precondition (lib/verb-set.sh).
# Before #891 the rule was a conjunction with `man/<name>.1`, and a HALF of
# it -- an executable with no page -- was silently discarded rather than
# reported: `ecosim-sensor` sat in that hole for its whole existence and
# surfaced instead as `ecosim-sensor-tick` reporting WRAPPER_NO_SENSOR, which
# read as a stale build and cost the misdiagnosis in realisateur#66.
# cut-verb-build.sh REFUSES on that shape still, but only in the direction
# that remains a defect: a man page with no executable beside it (a script
# that moved or was deleted, its doc left behind). An executable with no page
# is no longer a defect; it is a verb, and this file is now the ONLY way to
# keep one off PATH -- not a way to silence a refusal that no longer fires.
# THE TEST, Zach 2026-08-11, when this file blocked every nightly build:
#     "would another agent or Zach ever call one of those?"
# That is the question, and it is not the one the mechanical rule asks. The
# rule asks whether `bin/<name>` exists -- a fact about the tree. This asks
# whether the name is a FRONT DOOR: something a person or another project
# types. Everything else is an internal that happens to be executable, and an
# internal does not stop being one by qualifying mechanically.
# Applied, the test is usually obvious and usually already answered by the
# project's own shape: ecosim declares `sonde`, so `sonde` is the door and its
# instruments are behind it. When the answer is genuinely unclear, that IS the
# finding -- write down which way you decided and why, which is what every row
# below does.
# WHAT A ROW IS, AND IS NOT
#   IS      an executable that does a job of its own -- an installer, a cron
#           wrapper, a scraper, an archiver -- and would gain nothing from a
#           slot on PATH.
#   IS NOT  a genuine front door that merely has no page written yet. Ship it
#           as a verb with no page, or write the page -- a row here would
#           bury a real door permanently instead of documenting it.
# The distinguishing question, and it is not a matter of taste: would anyone
# ever type this name at a shell expecting the ecosystem's verb contract --
# `--help`, a page, a stable name on PATH? If yes it is a verb and it is
# missing its page. If no it gets a row.
# A row states the evidence it was judged on, in the file's own words where
# the file says so. `vim-arcade bin/sync-engine.sh` and `bibliothecaire
# bin/page92.py` both declare it themselves; the rest were judged by reading
# their headers on `bashified` on 2026-08-11, which is what the last column
# quotes.
# STALENESS IS VISIBLE IN THE ARTIFACT, not enforced here. Every row that
# ACTUALLY applies is written into the build manifest as a `# NOT-A-VERB` line,
# so a row that never appears in any manifest is a row about a file that is no
# longer there. Remove it when that happens: an exemption outliving its reason
# is how a temporary judgement becomes a permanent blind spot.
bibliothecaire
name: page92.py
why it is not a verb: a bounded public-domain scraper and gallery builder; its own docstring is its interface, and cut-verb-build.sh cites it as the canonical "executable, no page, exempted here rather than shipped" example (#891)

#project: vim-arcade
name: sync-engine.sh
why it is not a verb: says so in its own header: "NOT A VERB. It has no man/sync-engine.sh.1 and never will, so the declaration rule correctly does not count it"

#project: ecosim
name: silence-audit.sh

#project: ecosim
name: migration-watch.py
why it is not a verb: a one-purpose instrument for the mandark -> dexter migration: "OBSERVER ONLY ... writes nothing outside this repo, and cannot halt, gate or block a move"

#project: gardien
name: ecosystem-archive.sh

#project: scheduler
name: dose-project.sh
why it is not a verb: the implementation `bin/dose` execs for its project form, not a name anyone types: `dose ecosim`, never `dose-project.sh ecosim`. It travels on bashified only so the build carries it BESIDE bin/dose, which is what lets $SELF find it with no scheduler checkout and no exposure to hf7y/scheduler#99 -- see the dispatch comment in bin/dose. This row is what keeps it off PATH now that an executable alone would otherwise qualify it (#891).

#project: ecosim
name: ecosim-sensor
why it is not a verb: an instrument behind ecosim's actual verb `sonde`, not a door of its own -- Zach, 2026-08-11: "ecosim-sensor and ecosim-sweep are not verbs. ecosim's verb is sonde." It is machine-facing by construction: data on stdout, status-first lines so `grep '^BLIND'` works, stable fields so `awk` works, and Monitoring Plugins exit codes in which `--help` EXITS 3, not 0. A verb whose --help exits 3 fails the verb contract outright, which is mechanical confirmation of the judgement rather than a second opinion about it.

#project: ecosim
name: ecosim-sweep
why it is not a verb: the unattended one-pass driver over those instruments, run by a clock and read by a log, never typed -- same Zach ruling of 2026-08-11. Its contract is an aggregated severity (0 clean / 1 warn / 2 crit / 3 blind, BLIND beating CRIT), which is a thing a cron line consumes, not a thing a person asks for. `sonde` remains ecosim's one door.

#project: scheduler
name: freeze-check.sh
why it is not a verb: the migration abort handle `dose freeze-check` execs, carried onto bashified by hf7y/scheduler#123 so the dispatch path needs no checkout. Nobody types `freeze-check.sh`; they type `dose freeze-check`. It travels in the build to be BESIDE bin/dose, not to be on PATH.

#project: scheduler
name: verdict.sh
why it is not a verb: the verdict reader/writer behind `dose verdict`, carried by hf7y/scheduler#123. Its callers are the dispatcher and a project's own brief, never a person at a prompt -- and its whole contract is an exit code (0 DONE / 1 NOT-DONE / 3 GAVE-UP) consumed by a script, which is the shape of an internal rather than a door.

#project: scheduler
name: usage-paced-runner.sh
why it is not a verb: the dispatcher itself, carried by hf7y/scheduler#123. It is invoked by a cron tick, not by a human: `dose` is the door, this is the engine behind it. NOT a containment claim -- the build installs it 0775 at verb-builds/current/scheduler/bin/ on every account, so absence from PATH saves typing and prevents nothing. What bounds it is uid 0 for host mode (usage-paced-runner.sh:107-109), the usage gate, the flock, and PACED_MAX_PER_TICK.

#project: scheduler
name: tempo.sh
why it is not a verb: the pace regulator behind the dispatcher, not a door: its only caller is bin/usage-paced-runner.sh ("bin/tempo.sh decides how many of those asks become dispatches"), and `dose` names no `tempo` subcommand. Same shape as usage-paced-runner.sh above -- it travels on bashified so the dispatch path needs no scheduler checkout, not to be on PATH. Its header calls it "the thermostat's setpoint" (hf7y/scheduler#147); the knob a human actually edits is TEMPO_BASE_MIN, never this filename.

#project: scheduler
name: route-deliveries.sh
why it is not a verb: invoked by bin/scheduler-run:48 immediately before a dispatch, never typed; it routes a project's own deliveries and takes a --apply it is always given. A front door would be something a person runs on purpose, and nobody runs this except the runner

#project: scheduler
name: scheduler-run
why it is not a verb:
the batch dispatcher bin/usage-paced-runner.sh execs per rotation row, carried by hf7y/scheduler#433 so the dispatch path needs no clone. Its own header calls it HAND-RUN, and that is true and still not a verb: the hand-run it documents is `sudo -n -u

bash -lc 'cd ~/Documents/Projects/scheduler && bin/scheduler-run

batch'` -- invoked BY PATH out of a tree, never as a bare name expecting the verb contract. `dose ` is scheduler's door; this is the engine behind it, exactly as usage-paced-runner.sh above. It also takes no --help and its arguments are , a rotation row's two fields.

#project: scheduler
name: collect-feedback.sh
why it is not a verb: a text filter, not a door: lib/sweep-loop-common.sh:718 runs it over $HOME/reports/<project>/LATEST.md and splices the `%TAG` lines it finds into the run's prompt. Its own header states the contract a CALLER reads -- "exit 1 with NO output if the file has none ... a caller should read non-zero as 'nothing to say', not as an error" -- which is a convention between two scripts, not one a person types at. Carried with scheduler-run because its call site is `2>/dev/null || true`: absent, the human's inline feedback is dropped with no line in any log.

#project: senechal
name: selfdev-runner-provision.sh
why it is not a verb: a root crontab entry on monkey, alongside ausculte-cadence and selfdev-release-tick; it provisions CI runners for private repos and needs privileges no agent has. Zach types the account name, not this

#project: senechal
name: test-selfdev-runner-provision.sh
why it is not a verb: the witness for the row above. A test is never a verb; giving it a man page would declare a name whose only caller is a suite

#project: realisateur
name: monkey-watch.sh
why it is not a verb: the cron wrapper publishing hf7y.com/monkey from dexter, on bashified since #834 so it runs from the pin, not a `git pull` of main. #project: realisateur
name: monkey-status-collect.py
why it is not a verb: the collector monkey-watch.sh FEEDS to monkey over stdin (`sudo -n python3 -`), never invoked by name and deliberately never installed on the guest, so the version that runs is the one in the build. Beside monkey-watch.sh as scheduler's dose-project.sh is beside bin/dose
